title: Short Stuff: The NY Times Crossword
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the history of The New York Times crossword. They note the Times was the last major daily metropolitan newspaper to start a crossword, publishing its first only around World War II after roughly fifteen years of the crossword craze, reportedly because publisher Arthur Hays Sulzberger was tired of borrowing rival papers' puzzles. Margaret Farrar, who had edited Simon & Schuster crossword books, became the first editor and served 27 years (1942-1969), steering puzzles away from the day's news toward literature and pop culture. Will Wang succeeded her in 1969 and brought humor, Ziggy appearances and pun-style jokes; Eugene T. Maleska followed in 1977, making puzzles more sophisticated and serious. Will Shortz, the current editor, modernized the puzzle, brought in younger constructors, and is featured in the documentary Wordplay. The hosts also explain that puzzles are built by reverse engineering (theme answers first, then black squares, then clues), that the difficulty rises through the week from Monday to Saturday, and that the crossword subscription has close to half a million subscribers.

segments.title: Opening banter and the crossword's place in America
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the New York Times crossword, mention the documentary Wordplay featuring Will Shortz and Jon Stewart, and call Shortz a legendary current editor.

segments.title: Late start and the World War II debut
segments.summary: The Times was the last major US daily metropolitan paper to start a crossword, despite a crossword craze starting about 1920s. Publisher Arthur Hays Sulzberger reportedly wanted his own puzzle instead of borrowing rivals', and it debuted around World War II.

segments.title: Margaret Farrar and the first editor
segments.summary: Margaret Farrar, who had edited Simon & Schuster crossword books, became the Times' first crossword editor. She first was asked to tie clues to the day's news, then pushed for literature and pop culture references, and served 27 years, from 1942 to 1969.

segments.title: Will Wang and Eugene Maleska
segments.summary: Will Wang, a former Metropolitan desk head, took over in 1969 and brought humor, including frequent Ziggy appearances. Eugene T. Maleska followed in 1977, with more sophisticated, serious puzzles.

segments.title: Will Shortz and the modernized puzzle
segments.summary: Will Shortz is described as combining the strengths of earlier editors. He modernized the puzzle, brought in younger constructors (average contributor age fell from the early fifties to about the thirties), and receives about 70 submissions a week.

segments.title: How crosswords are built and their difficulty
segments.summary: Constructors typically place theme answers first, then black squares, then clues. The Monday puzzle is easiest and Saturday hardest, with Sunday larger but about Wednesday or Thursday difficulty.

segments.title: Online subscription and personal crossword habits
segments.summary: The NYT crossword has close to half a million subscribers, a notable income source. Hosts discuss their own crossword habits, including Chicago Tribune and in-flight puzzles.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck recommend the documentary Wordplay and sign off with a credit for iHeartRadio and HowStuffWorks.
